evaluation.positioning_hook: A self-doubting Midwestern teen discovers she’s a shapeshifting child experiment trapped in a corporate cover-up, and must outrun the people who made her before they erase who she really is.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, movie-trailer engine: a teen discovers she can become anyone she touches, and the story keeps turning that power into danger, identity panic, and escape. The audience is real and commercial, though the body-horror and existential identity angle narrow it from four-quadrant to genre-forward streaming/theatrical specialty.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast in the opening chase and then sharpens in the school and mall sequences: Ava is not just hiding from a company, she is the company’s missing shapeshifter. The script keeps the premise legible even as it layers in memory theft, body-copying, and the Ava/Madison reveal.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison is a strong lead because her insecurity, intelligence, and moral instinct all play against the same pressure. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and David are vivid enough to support the engine, though the script is still most magnetic when it’s centered on Ava’s internal conflict.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar chase-thriller frame and makes the central mechanic emotional: identity is not metaphorical, it is literal, transferable, and weaponized. The repeated body-swaps, the memory contamination, and the final Ava/Madison inversion give it a confident, unusual shape.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with real escalation: cold open chase, school intrusion, first transformation, reveal of the company, then the identity collapse and lab siege. Each major sequence changes the rules or the stakes, and the final act keeps tightening rather than stalling.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a girl who thinks she’s Ava but is actually Madison, with a second girl living inside the same identity ecosystem, is both surprising and emotionally inevitable once the rules are clear. The script’s strongest originality comes from making class, self-worth, and bodily autonomy all collide inside one sci-fi premise.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The town, the company security presence, the school, the mall, and the secret lab all feel like parts of one social machine. The world is story-generating, though it remains intentionally contained around the cover-up rather than expanding into a larger civic or institutional ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is a distinctive mix of teen awkwardness, paranoid sci-fi, and emotional body-horror, with jokes and domestic texture sitting right next to panic and mutation. The Ava/June banter and the transformation scenes give it a voice that feels specific rather than generic genre.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the thriller mechanics there’s a deeper engine about self-hatred, class resentment, maternal love, and the violence of being seen incorrectly. The script hints at a larger moral universe, but it stays focused on the immediate survival story rather than opening out into broader thematic mystery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ava and June have a strong, combustible mother-daughter dynamic, Shannon gives the teen world a real social anchor, and David/Priscilla/Wolcott create a memorable antagonist triangle. It’s not an ensemble piece in the broad sense, but the relationships do generate recurring story energy.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: female, teen (16), high-school student; later revealed to be Madison in Ava’s body/identity
lead_characters.hook: Ava is the script’s emotional center: bright, self-conscious, morally stubborn, and desperate to believe she can be more than the girl she thinks she is. What starts as a teen-insecurity story becomes a crisis of identity when she learns she is actually Madison, a child shapeshifter whose memories were overwritten by the Ava persona; the role lives in the collision between fear, intelligence, and a fierce instinct to do the right thing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory like Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve when the role lets an actor play wit, vulnerability, and identity fracture in the same breath. It gives a young performer a full emotional arc, plus the physical challenge of multiple bodies and the dramatic turn of realizing the self you’ve been performing is not the self you are.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.hook: June is a hard-edged, funny, overextended single mom who looks like she’s improvising adulthood one shift at a time, but she’s far more capable than Ava gives her credit for. She’s emotionally messy, economically cornered, and unexpectedly fierce once the danger becomes physical; the reveal that she can shapeshift too turns her from frazzled parent into a survivalist with a secret history.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the lived-in volatility of Frances McDormand in Nomadland or Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April, then adds action and genre surprise. It’s a mother role with bite, humor, and a late-breaking physical transformation payoff.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the loyal, funny best friend who keeps the teen world grounded while also functioning as Ava’s reality check. She’s socially smart, emotionally direct, and the kind of supporting character who can carry both comic relief and genuine concern without feeling ornamental.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of best-friend role that gives an actor the sharp, scene-stealing support of Beanie Feldstein in Lady Bird or Auli’i Cravalho in Crush. It offers comic timing, friendship chemistry, and a chance to be the audience’s grounded entry point into the chaos.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the polished, ruthless face of the cover-up: calm in public, predatory in private, and always one step away from turning charm into coercion. She’s not a cartoon villain; she’s a professional who believes she’s managing a necessary evil, which makes her more dangerous and more playable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong antagonist material in the vein of Laura Linney in Ozark or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers when the role lets an actor weaponize intelligence and composure. It gives a performer authority, menace, and the chance to make corporate cruelty feel personal.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: male, elderly (90), shapeshifter; also appears in younger copied forms
lead_characters.hook: David is the tragic counterpoint to Ava: a broken, elderly shapeshifter whose identity has been splintered by captivity, memory loss, and survival instinct. He can be tender, manipulative, frightened, and dangerous in the same scene, and his bond with Madison gives the script its strangest emotional core.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that recalls Paul Dano in Prisoners or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom when an actor gets to play damaged intelligence under pressure. It also offers a rare transformation-heavy performance opportunity, with emotional continuity across radically different bodies.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.demographics: male, late 20s to 30s, security operative, ex-military
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the most human of the company muscle: competent, wary, and visibly uncomfortable with the job even as he keeps doing it. He’s a pressure-release valve inside the antagonist machine, and the script gives him just enough conscience to make his eventual turn feel earned.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, conflicted enforcer role that lets an actor play against type the way Shea Whigham or Scoot McNairy often do. It’s a solid showcase for restraint, moral fatigue, and a late-breaking pivot.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument of the operation: intimidating, procedural, and always ready to escalate. He’s less psychologically complex than Priscilla or Wolcott, but he gives the story a reliable physical threat and a face for the chase.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is dependable heavy territory in the mold of Michael Shannon in supporting antagonist mode or Walton Goggins when he’s playing controlled menace. It gives an actor authority, physicality, and a clean villain function.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.hook: Wilma is the softer, more ambiguous face of the system, which makes her useful and unsettling at once. She presents as caring and practical, but she’s still part of the machinery that manipulates the shapeshifters, and the script uses her to complicate the moral map.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play warmth with a hidden edge, like Rebecca Hall in The Night House when the performance is all about controlled unease. It offers a chance to be sympathetic without being innocent.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the cold, self-justifying architect of the whole nightmare, a man who talks like a visionary while behaving like a sadist. He’s the script’s clearest embodiment of power without empathy, and his scenes give the story its most overtly monstrous energy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige-villain territory in the vein of Bryan Cranston in Your Honor or Michael Keaton in Spotlight when the role lets an actor weaponize intelligence and entitlement. It offers a big, scene-commanding antagonist with ideological self-belief.

casting_characteristics: teen lead with strong emotional range
multiple body/identity forms for the same characters
supporting roles with age-specific casting across teens, 20s, 40s, and 60s

technical.vfx_details: Repeated shapeshift transformations, body-morphing effects, skin bubbling, and a few fire/foam interaction beats; mostly character-driven but effects-dependent in key scenes.
technical.sfx_needs: Cattle prods, tasers, gunfire, vehicle chase beats, practical foam effects, fire/sprinkler sequence, and controlled injury makeup.

rights_flags.detail: Eric Huntington is a fictional billionaire character, but the script also references a New York Times reporter and a dead billionaire in Mexico as part of the cover story; no life-rights issue is triggered by name alone.
TikTok is referenced as the platform where shapeshifter videos are buried in AI slop.
Trader Joe’s is named in the mall escape sequence.
The New York Times is named in the final reporting beat.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: genre-forward theatrical or streaming original with strong teen/young-adult audience appeal and premium-cable-level content tolerance.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the script depends on repeated transformation effects, a mall sequence, a secret-lab climax, practical foam/fire work, and multiple night chase setups.

casting.note: The lead has to play teen insecurity, moral force, physical transformation, and identity fracture; June, Priscilla, and Wolcott also need actors who can carry both realism and genre escalation.

development.note: The Ava/Madison reveal is the script’s strongest twist, but it also asks the audience to track a lot of identity logic, memory contamination, and body-copy rules without losing emotional clarity.

comp_set.title: Freaky
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the body-swap identity engine and the comic-horror tension of a character trapped in the wrong body while trying to survive escalating danger.

comp_set.title: The Faculty
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the small-town teen paranoia, secret-invasion energy, and the way the school becomes a pressure cooker for a larger sci-fi threat.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on contained suspense and the slow realization that the social environment is hiding a much darker system underneath.

comp_set.title: Upgrade
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the high-concept body-control premise and the efficient, propulsive genre storytelling that turns a single mechanic into escalating set pieces.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre audiences who like smart, emotional sci-fi thrillers with a teen lead, plus viewers drawn to identity-driven body-horror and found-family stakes.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 16-34, with a meaningful female audience and strong YA-to-adult crossover; best for viewers comfortable with elevated genre and moderate violence.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary small-town settings keep it contained, but the transformation effects, chase sequences, and lab climax push it above true micro-budget.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams buying elevated-genre female leads
boutique genre financiers looking for contained high-concept features
indie producers with a track record in teen-adjacent suspense
director-driven companies seeking a breakout showcase role
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character emotion and a clean sci-fi hook do equal work. It has enough commercial propulsion for genre buyers, but the identity/memory angle gives it the prestige texture that helps it travel beyond pure effects-driven fare.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the Ava/Madison story resolves cleanly, and there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector with a supporting character deep enough to anchor a separate project.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hook is immediate and visual.
strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one breath: a teen discovers she can become anyone she touches while a corporate cleanup crew hunts her. That clarity is a real commercial asset because it makes the trailer, poster, and pitch all easy to sell.
strengths.evidence: The opening woods chase, the first body change in the alley, and the later school/mall reveals all deliver the premise cleanly and repeatedly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Identity is the engine, not just the premise.
strengths.what_it_means: The script turns a sci-fi mechanic into a performance role about self-worth, class shame, and the terror of being seen incorrectly. That gives the project a stronger buyer case than a standard chase thriller because it can attract both genre and prestige-minded audiences.
strengths.evidence: Ava’s insecurity about her body, the Ava/Madison reveal, and the final note about not being made out of love all deepen the concept.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother-daughter bond gives it emotional ballast.
strengths.what_it_means: June keeps the movie from becoming a pure concept exercise; she gives the story a second emotional spine and a built-in audience hook. That matters commercially because it broadens the appeal beyond teen genre fans into adult viewers who respond to family stakes.
strengths.evidence: June’s banter, her late reveal as a shapeshifter, and the final found-family alignment with Madison all pay off that relationship.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The transformation set pieces are built for showcase.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives actors and effects teams repeated moments to turn identity into spectacle, which is exactly what helps a genre title stand out in a crowded market. It also creates a clear reason for a director or performer to attach: the movie promises scenes people will talk about.
strengths.evidence: The mall bathroom transformation, the Ava/Christy swap, the Ava/Eric sequence, and the final fire/foam mutation climax.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The antagonist system feels legible and saleable.
strengths.what_it_means: Priscilla, Wolcott, Jamieson, and the company apparatus create a clean corporate-conspiracy lane that buyers know how to market. That gives the script a dependable genre frame while still leaving room for character nuance.
strengths.evidence: The school intrusion, the secret lab, the settlement language, and the investor call all make the operation feel like a real machine.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, high-concept sci-fi thriller with a real performance engine: a teen identity crisis that becomes a body-swap survival story. The premise is easy to market, the emotional stakes are legible, and the production footprint stays in a buyable indie lane even with the effects-heavy climax.

items.area: The Ava/Madison reveal is doing a lot of work.
items.detail: The script asks the audience to track a long chain of identity substitutions, memory contamination, and body-copy rules before the final truth lands. That’s a strong twist, but it is also the main comprehension risk in the package and the thing a buyer will test hardest in notes.

items.area: The third act leans on exposition in the lab.
items.detail: Once the story reaches the secret facility, several scenes shift into explanation mode: Wolcott’s philosophy, the investors, the treatment rules, and the deal structure. The material is clear enough, but the back half becomes more declarative than the earlier chase sections, which slightly softens momentum.

items.area: The effects and stunt load are not trivial.
items.detail: Repeated shapeshifts, foam burns, cattle prods, gunfire, a fire/sprinkler climax, and multiple night chase beats mean this is not a cheap contained thriller. It still lives in indie territory, but buyers will need to plan for effects execution rather than assuming a dialogue-driven package.

items.area: The lead role narrows casting more than it first appears.
items.detail: Ava/Madison has to play teen insecurity, comic timing, moral clarity, physical fear, and then the destabilization of realizing she is not who she thought she was. That is a strong role, but it is a demanding one, and the movie’s success will depend on finding an actor who can carry both the emotional and genre sides without flattening either.

items.area: The company conspiracy is familiar territory.
items.detail: Corporate cover-up, private security, secret lab, investor pressure, and a visionary villain are all effective, but they sit in a well-traveled sci-fi-thriller lane. The script’s differentiator is the identity mechanic; the buyer conversation will still include how much of the familiar conspiracy frame is needed versus how much is there to support the premise.

issues.headline: The biggest friction point is comprehension around the Ava/Madison identity stack: it’s the movie’s best twist and its biggest buyer test. Beyond that, the back half becomes more explanatory than the opening run, and the effects/casting demands are real enough that this is a smart indie, not a casual one.
